A lump sum or phased purchases: chart the investment and the cash waiting beside it

Compare two schedules for capital already available, include interest on waiting cash, and see how rising and falling return assumptions change the result.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two schedules for money already available

Interactive planning lab

All-at-once final total, including cash$67,416
Phased final total, including waiting-cash interest$66,861.61
Phased minus all-at-once final value-$554.39

Hypothetical money is fully available at time zero. Both paths use the same capital and common endpoint. All-at-once buys before the first month’s return. Phased purchases occur before each of the first selected months’ returns, in equal portions of original capital. Cash earns its own effective annual assumed return converted monthly, after that month’s purchase; interest stays in cash and is never added to a later purchase. Asset returns are also effective annual assumptions converted monthly. Every total includes both the investment and remaining cash. No outside contributions, withdrawals, transaction fees, taxes, bid-ask spread, inflation, currency change or account limits. Constant-return paths are controlled examples, not market data, forecasts, probabilities or evidence that one schedule always wins.

The central idea

A fair timing comparison starts with the same available capital, includes all waiting cash and ends on the same date. A smooth scenario explains the arithmetic; it does not establish which future market path will occur.

01

First establish whether the money exists today

Investing from each future paycheque and deciding what to do with an existing lump sum are different planning questions. In the first case, future earnings are not yet available. In the second, the full amount can be assigned now, and any phased schedule leaves part of it waiting in cash.

Investor.gov defines dollar-cost averaging as making equal purchases at regular intervals regardless of market movements. This guide uses that scheduling idea for capital already on hand. It does not assume the household can invest wages before earning them.

The default begins with CAD 60,000. The all-at-once case buys before the first month’s investment return. The phased case makes six CAD 10,000 purchases at the beginning of six consecutive months. No new capital arrives from outside the comparison, and neither case withdraws spending money during the horizon.

02

Purchase principal and investment value are different lines

The first chart tracks cumulative original capital assigned to purchases. All-at-once deployment reaches CAD 60,000 immediately. Six-purchase deployment assigns CAD 10,000 initially and another CAD 10,000 at each of the next five monthly purchase dates. The sixth purchase completes the schedule five months after the first.

This chart does not show market value. If an investment declines after purchase, cumulative purchase principal remains unchanged while investment value falls. A deployed-capital line is useful for understanding exposure timing but cannot tell the reader how much the account is currently worth.

The second chart answers that valuation question by adding the investment to cash still held beside it. Both totals begin at CAD 60,000. Comparing only the invested portion would omit a resource that the phased case still owns and make the comparison inconsistent. Waiting cash has its own entered return assumption rather than silently earning either the asset return or zero.

03

Give waiting cash an explicit interest rule

The default investment return is an assumed 6% effective annual rate and waiting cash earns an assumed 2% effective annual rate. Both are converted to equivalent monthly compounded rates. Purchases occur before the month’s growth and cash-interest calculation.

Each planned purchase uses only CAD 10,000 of original principal. Interest earned on waiting cash stays in the cash account. It is not silently added to the next purchase or transferred into the asset when the sixth purchase occurs. It continues to earn the selected cash return to the common endpoint.

At twenty-four months, the all-at-once investment is CAD 67,416 with no separate cash balance. The phased investment is about CAD 66,604.85, plus CAD 256.76 in retained cash interest, giving a combined CAD 66,861.61. Phased minus all-at-once is about negative CAD 554.39. Comparing only the investment values would overstate this particular difference by omitting the interest account.

04

Change the path before declaring a winner

The grouped bars repeat the calculation with smooth annual investment returns of negative 10%, zero and positive 10%. The selected cash return, capital, purchase count and horizon remain the same. Those alternatives demonstrate how the direction of the investment return changes the effect of waiting.

When the asset grows faster than cash along these smooth paths, delaying part of the purchase reduces time earning the higher rate. When the asset declines, the part still in cash avoids that earlier asset decline. Neither statement establishes the outcome of a volatile real market. A path that falls and then recovers can differ from a smooth path with the same final price.

FINRA discusses both the potential benefits and limitations of gradual purchases, including the return trade-off from holding cash and the distinction between existing funds and money invested as it is earned. The charts illustrate those mechanics with invented inputs. They do not reproduce a backtest or estimate how often either schedule succeeds.

05

Read the signed matrix as a conditional difference

Every matrix cell subtracts the all-at-once final total from a phased final total. Positive amounts mean the phased alternative finishes larger under that cell’s assumptions; negative amounts mean it finishes smaller. Rows change the assumed annual investment return and columns change the number of equal purchases.

The final date remains fixed. A twelve-purchase case is not allowed twelve extra months beyond the three-purchase case. Likewise, increasing the purchase count does not add more initial capital. It divides the same original sum into smaller transfers. With a one-purchase schedule, the two modeled paths are identical; this is an accounting check rather than an investment conclusion.

The model excludes transaction costs, taxes and bid-ask spreads. More trades could change costs where a provider charges per transaction. Cash yields and investment returns can also change during implementation. Account restrictions, currency conversion and whether a holding is appropriate for the goal require separate information. The tool assumes fractional purchases are possible and does not price individual shares.

06

Use the comparison to specify a plan that can be followed

Before selecting a timing rule, separate cash needed for near-term bills from money assigned to the investment goal. A schedule comparison cannot establish that the original capital is affordable to invest or that the selected asset has appropriate risk. A smooth positive line is an assumption, not a promise of capital protection.

If a phased schedule is used, write down the amount, purchase dates, treatment of cash interest and a review rule. Repeatedly postponing scheduled purchases after each market move creates a different strategy from the fixed schedule shown here. If the intended purchase is stopped, the uninvested cash and its opportunity cost still belong in the comparison.

Read the four charts as a sequence: when principal is deployed, what all resources are worth, how alternative market directions change the result, and how sensitive the final difference is to purchase count. The useful output is a transparent explanation of exposure timing. Choosing a schedule still requires a goal, an appropriate holding and a realistic ability to follow the plan.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All four charts use original deterministic return assumptions. They contain no historical returns, empirical success rate, probability distribution or recommended investment schedule.
